text: sudo's privileges all trace back to one file: /etc/sudoers. This lesson goes past sudo just existing into how to actually read a sudoers line, how to hand a user one specific command instead of full root, and why you edit this file with visudo and never with a plain text editor.

A sudoers line reads who, where, as whom, what. root ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL and percent-sudo ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL are the defaults on almost every install — a user or a percent-prefixed group, applying on any host, running as root, allowed to run any command at all. That's full sudo access, and it's rarely what a real grant should hand out.

Break that line into four pieces. Who is the user or group being granted access. Where is the host the rule applies on, since one sudoers file can be shared across many servers. As whom is which user the command actually runs as, almost always root. And what is the exact command list allowed — ALL meaning everything, or a short list meaning just that.

jsmith ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx grants exactly one command as root and nothing else — least privilege applied to sudo itself. Adding NOPASSWD: skips the password re-prompt for that rule, which is why automation accounts use it so a deploy script can call sudo without a human typing a password — never a real interactive account, since it removes sudo's one remaining check.

Commands in sudoers are always absolute paths, like /usr/bin/systemctl, never just systemctl — sudo won't trust $PATH for a privileged command, closing off an attacker planting a fake binary earlier in someone's path. And because /etc/sudoers controls access to fix /etc/sudoers, a typo saved with a plain editor can lock out sudo for everyone. visudo validates the grammar before it writes, refusing a bad save outright.

Most real sudo grants don't even live in the main file — they drop into /etc/sudoers.d/ as focused, single-purpose files, edited just as safely with visudo -f. Next up: PAM, the framework login, sudo, and ssh all authenticate through.
